body:
Thanks for the report -- I was able to reproduce this issue.

I'm not sure what the correct fix for this should be. Two problems are getting autofixed here (`semi` and `no-extra-semi` both remove extra semicolons), and both fixes are independently correct. However, the behavior of the code changes when both fixes are applied simultaneously. We might need to make the conflict detection more strict in [`source-code-fixer`](https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/7e04b33028e68555c69cf2568d606cdeab0b7cda/lib/util/source-code-fixer.js).

**What changes did you make? (Give an overview)**

`semi(never)` will remove current semicolon if the following token is also a semicolon. `no-extra-semi`  will also remove current semicolon if the previous token is a semicolon.

If there is no whitespace between two semicolons, it is safe because `SourceCodeFixer` don't fix two contacted problem. I add verification of whether the previous semi contacts with the current one in `no-extra-semi`.

How to test two rules at the same time and where to put the test file.

Thank you for the report.

> We might need to make the conflict detection more strict in source-code-fixer.

I agree.
Or, maybe we can revisit #3885.

> Two problems are getting autofixed here (semi and no-extra-semi both remove extra semicolons), and both fixes are independently correct. However, the behavior of the code changes when both fixes are applied simultaneously. 

I think we should remove the overlapping behaviour from `semi`.

Sorry @not-an-aardvark, after re-reading the original issue I think I misinterpreted it. I'm still not sure it's an autofixing issue, rather than a reporting issue in the first place (I think there is just one problem in the context of the program, not two), but I'm not sure how I would prevent that. Except by merging the rules, as @mysticatea mentioned.

Anyhow, I think one approach to avoid the conflicting fixes would be to consider the range including both semicolons as part of the fix in `no-extra-semi`.

Do you have something in mind regarding `source-code-fixer`?

> Do you have something in mind regarding `source-code-fixer`?

I think we could fix issues like this by making conflict detection more strict. We currently detect conflicts between fixes based on whether their ranges overlap -- maybe we could change that to detect conflicts ~~if there are any tokens~~ between the ranges.

edit: I meant to say that conflicts should be detected if there *aren't* any tokens between the ranges.

body:
This also came up in #8026, where no-else-return and no-useless-return have independently-correct fixes that together break the code.

I'd be happy to help contribute a fix to this if there's agreement on the approach (or at least happy to brainstorm solutions).

Reading through the code a bit, here's my understanding of how all this stuff works (please correct me if I'm missing/misunderstanding anything):

* Each rule optionally advertises one fix of the form (start, end, text), meaning that the range from start to end should be replaced with the text.
* The code in source-code-fixer.js applies as many of these as it can, working backwards, and ignores any fixes that happen on overlapping ranges.
* The `multipassFix` function in cli-engine.js re-runs eslint and all fixes over and over, up to 10 times, until no more fixing can be done. This generally means that any fixes will make it through eventually, even if there are some conflicts.

My impression is that we need to extend the autofixer API in some way, since it seems impossible for source-code-fixer to have enough context as-is to know if two changes are incompatible.

Here's one idea: in addition to returning the start, end, and text, any rule can optionally specify a range of code that must not be touched in the same pass.
* no-extra-semi and semi could maybe specify the entire range between the preceding and following statements (so that we don't remove two semicolons in a row).
* no-useless-return and maybe no-else-return could specify the entire function body, since any change to the control flow could cause correctness issues.

That would force the autofixes to be applied independently, which I think fixes both of these cases.

I guess another approach might be to just make the replacement bigger for these rules, e.g. no-useless-return would replace the entire function body with the same function body minus the `return`. That would fix things without needing any changes to source-code-fixer and without needing any changes to the fix format. I guess a downside to this is that it seems pretty subtle and non-obvious, so it would at least need better documentation for rule-writers, and maybe an extension to the rule-fixer API to make it easier.

@alangpierce Your analysis of how autofixing works is basically correct. One additional note: fixable rules also must export a `meta.fixable` property, which has a value of either `code` or `whitespace`. (At the moment, the property isn't actually used for anything, but it was introduced in case we ever needed to filter fixes to avoid conflicts, e.g. by only applying fixes that don't affect the AST.)

Your idea of specifying a "don't touch this code" range for fixes seems like it would work. My main concern is that it might be difficult for a rule author to think of all the possible conflicting fixes that could cause a problem. I like that the current autofixing system doesn't have much mental overhead -- a rule can (supposedly) just convert code to other valid code, and assume that core will take care of any conflicts.

---

Here are a few other possibilities (some of which might have their own issues, but listed for the sake of brainstorming):

1. Automatically infer the conflict range based on the range of the reported node. (This is similar to your suggestion of using larger fix ranges. I think your suggestion is probably better, because this would tightly couple the report range with the internal fix logic.)
1. Infer the conflict range based on something else from a rule, such as the nodes that the rule listens for. (Since rules can use `parent` properties or `sourceCode.ast`, this probably wouldn't be reliable.)
1. Give up on trying to detect conflicts, and reparse after applying every fix. (This has all the desirable qualities that we would want, except that the performance would probably be unacceptable.)
1. Include metadata about fixes and the AST when detecting conflicts. For example, I would assume we can be more liberal about fixes that don't modify the AST, or fixes that only modify whitespace. (If we can figure out a good way to do this, I think it would be the best solution.)

@ilyavolodin I think both fixes would still happen in your example (if I'm understanding things right). All that the locking would ensure is that the two fixes aren't applied *in the same pass*. In this case, the source-code-fixer code would pick either `linebreak-style` or `semi` to apply in the first pass, and skip the other, and in the second pass, the other fix would be detected and applied.

This might make eslint slower on average (e.g. 3 or 4 passes instead of 2) and more likely to hit the 10 pass limit, but my impression is that it won't be a really big deal, and that correctness for autofixing is really important.
